title: Competing specialist orders
stem: A stable client with heart failure and diarrhoeal losses has a 1500 mL/day fluid limit from cardiology and a 2000 mL/day limit from medicine, both entered this morning. Breakfast fluids are due. What should the nurse do?
options: Use 1500 mL/day because the stricter limit seems safer
Use 2000 mL/day because medicine entered its order later
Contact the coordinating practitioner to reconcile today's fluid plan
Continue yesterday's 1800 mL/day limit until routine rounds
why: The stricter limit may worsen the competing volume-depletion problem.
Entry time alone does not reconcile the two clinical intentions.
The nurse needs one authorized plan balancing congestion risk and current losses.
Yesterday's limit does not resolve today's conflicting active instructions.
takeaway: Resolve conflicting active orders through coordinated clarification.
learningObjective: Resolve conflicting active orders through coordinated clarification.

title: Unmet refrigeration need
stem: A client's prescribed unopened injectable product must remain at 2–8°C according to its label. Their home has no refrigeration; the pharmacy can store it and dispense the scheduled dose during a daily visit the client can reliably attend. What is best?
options: Teach the client to keep the full supply in an ordinary picnic cooler
Ask a neighbour who is away weekdays to refrigerate the full supply
Collect the month's supply and refrigerate it only before each injection
Confirm the pharmacy storage and scheduled dispensing arrangement with the care team
why: An ordinary cooler has no verified ability to maintain the labelled range.
The neighbour's absence makes timely access unreliable.
Intermittent refrigeration does not meet continuous storage requirements.
The available arrangement meets both storage and reliable access needs.
takeaway: Assess whether treatment requirements can be met after discharge.
learningObjective: Assess whether treatment requirements can be met after discharge.

title: Home-care entry plan
stem: A consenting postoperative client cannot reach the door. A wound visit is booked for 0900; the authorized key holder works until 1700, but a service-approved lockbox can be installed today. What should the nurse coordinate?
options: Confirm consented lockbox access with the client and visiting service
Ask the key holder to bring the key after work that day
Replace the scheduled wound assessment with telephone instructions
Move the visit to evening despite the time-sensitive morning care plan
why: The lockbox provides authorized access at the required visit time.
The key holder's availability does not match the morning appointment.
Telephone coaching cannot replace the scheduled hands-on assessment.
Changing timing may leave the prescribed time-sensitive care unmet.
takeaway: Plan practical access before essential home-care visits.
learningObjective: Plan practical access before essential home-care visits.

title: Interpreter confidentiality concern
stem: A client declines a local interpreter because they know them socially and fear disclosure. What should the nurse arrange?
options: Continue because interpreters sign confidentiality agreements
Offer another qualified interpreter, including remote options
Ask the local interpreter to persuade the client
Use the client's limited English for the complex decision
why: Formal confidentiality does not remove the expressed barrier to participation.
An alternative can preserve language access and the client's comfort.
Persuasion by the person of concern may deepen mistrust.
Complex decision-making still requires effective communication.
takeaway: Address interpreter concerns while preserving language access.
learningObjective: Address interpreter concerns while preserving language access.

title: Aphasia and choice
stem: After stroke, a client follows spoken instructions and gives accurate single yes/no responses when allowed ten seconds. Speech remains effortful. Which approaches support reliable participation? Select all that apply.
options: Allow the demonstrated response time before moving on
Ask several yes/no questions together to reduce visit time
Offer one clearly presented visual choice at a time
Supply the likely answer immediately when speech pauses
why: The known response delay should be accommodated rather than treated as inability.
Bundled questions make it unclear which answer the client intends.
Single choices reduce expressive demands while preserving the client's own response.
Premature completion can replace the client's intended answer with the nurse's assumption.
takeaway: Distinguish impaired expression from inability to participate.
learningObjective: Distinguish impaired expression from inability to participate.

title: Conflicting discharge lists
stem: A fracture client's discharge letter says clinic review on 12 October, but an automated text says 19 October. The surgeon requested review within one week of the 6 October discharge. What should the nurse do?
options: Use the letter because it meets the requested interval
Use the automated message because it arrived most recently
Verify the booked appointment and required interval with the clinic
Advise attendance on 12 October even if booking is unconfirmed
why: The letter may contain the intended date but does not establish an accepted booking.
A newer message may still reflect a scheduling error.
Clinic verification resolves both timing and the actual appointment arrangement.
Arriving for an unconfirmed slot may not provide the required review.
takeaway: Resolve contradictory transition instructions before relying on them.
learningObjective: Resolve contradictory transition instructions before relying on them.

title: Emergency contact versus consent
stem: An alert client can discuss a proposed treatment change and is available at bedside. Their neighbour, listed as emergency contact, asks to approve it. Which response is best?
options: I will discuss the decision directly with the client
I will first check whether you hold a separate representation document
I will ask you which option the client would probably prefer
I will wait until the client's usual family contact arrives
why: The capable available client should participate directly in the treatment decision.
Substitute-document review is not the first step when the capable client is available.
The neighbour's knowledge may support discussion but does not replace the client's choice.
Family availability need not delay this capable client's decision.
takeaway: Do not confuse communication contacts with decision-makers.
learningObjective: Do not confuse communication contacts with decision-makers.

title: Care refusal and dependence
stem: A client declines a shower but accepts washing at the sink. Staff describe the client as refusing all hygiene. What should the nurse do?
options: Clarify the accepted alternative and adapt the care plan
Schedule a mandatory shower before breakfast
Record total refusal because the shower was planned
Ask family to persuade acceptance of the shower
why: The client is selecting a different way to meet the care need.
A routine schedule does not override a capable preference.
The record should reflect accepted and declined care accurately.
Persuasion is unnecessary before considering the reasonable alternative.
takeaway: Distinguish refusal of one method from refusal of the care goal.
learningObjective: Distinguish refusal of one method from refusal of the care goal.

title: Client-held medicines list
stem: A client says they stopped a medicine after a telephone instruction. The last discharge list includes it, the pharmacy recently dispensed it, and tablets remain at home. What best resolves reconciliation?
options: Use the dispensing history as proof the medicine is still being taken
Clarify the client's actual use and verify the reported instruction with prescribing records
Use the last discharge list because it is an official document
Count the remaining tablets and infer the current prescribed schedule
why: Dispensing shows supply, not actual use or a later discontinuation.
Both real use and the authorized treatment plan need clarification.
A discharge list may predate the reported telephone change.
Tablet count cannot establish the prescriber's current intention.
takeaway: Reconcile actual medication use using more than one reliable source.
learningObjective: Reconcile actual medication use using more than one reliable source.

title: Shared care ownership
stem: Agency A performs dressings daily; Agency B manages equipment. Only three dressing kits remain, and delivery takes two days. Each agency thinks the other orders supplies. Which actions help? Select all that apply.
options: Ask both agencies to order full supplies independently
Agree on one ordering lead and a reorder threshold
Record and share who checks stock and confirms delivery
Route routine kit requests through a clinic with a one-week turnaround
why: Duplicate ordering may create confusion and waste without clear accountability.
A lead and threshold match stock levels to delivery time.
Shared ownership details support follow-through across services.
That pathway cannot meet the immediate supply timeline.
takeaway: Assign responsibility across services explicitly.
learningObjective: Assign responsibility across services explicitly.

title: Missed interpreter booking
stem: A stable client needs complex discharge teaching today. A qualified telephone interpreter is available now; an in-person interpreter is available in three days. The client agrees to telephone interpretation. What is best?
options: Use a translated leaflet alone and complete discharge today
Use a demonstration video and ask for a signature afterward
Conduct interactive teaching through the telephone interpreter and verify understanding
Use a bilingual employee whose interpreting competence is unknown
why: A leaflet cannot answer the client's treatment-specific questions or verify understanding.
A generic video does not provide an interactive communication channel.
The available qualified service permits timely two-way teaching acceptable to the client.
Language ability alone does not establish competence for complex interpretation.
takeaway: Resolve language access before relying on complex teaching.
learningObjective: Resolve language access before relying on complex teaching.

title: Nonurgent family call during crisis
stem: While assessing a deteriorating client, a nurse receives a routine family-update call about another client. An authorized unit clerk is available to verify callback details and schedule contact after stabilization. What is best?
options: Interrupt assessment to provide the full update immediately
Forward the caller to the prescriber who is attending the same emergency
Ask the caller to repeatedly phone the desk until the nurse is free
Delegate the approved callback arrangements and continue the urgent assessment
why: A routine update should not interrupt urgent clinical assessment.
That transfer may distract another essential emergency responder.
Repeated calls do not establish a reliable follow-up plan.
Available support can preserve communication follow-up while urgent care continues.
takeaway: Coordinate routine communication while protecting urgent clinical work.
learningObjective: Coordinate routine communication while protecting urgent clinical work.

title: Unexpected absence of caregiver
stem: A client needs hands-on supervision for every transfer. Their planned caregiver is hospitalized on discharge morning, and the client will be alone after transport leaves. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask the transition coordinator to arrange temporary support before discharge
Ask transport staff to assist with the first transfer at home
Request the first home-care visit later the following afternoon
Repeat the transfer demonstration before sending the client home
why: The changed plan needs support covering ongoing transfers, not only arrival.
One transfer does not address later toileting and mobility needs.
The client would remain unsupported through the intervening period.
Teaching does not replace the required hands-on supervision.
takeaway: Reassess discharge readiness when essential support changes.
learningObjective: Reassess discharge readiness when essential support changes.

title: Visit priority in home care
stem: During a home-care call, a caregiver reports that the client opens their eyes only briefly to shaking, cannot answer, and is breathing. A glucose meter is in another room. What is the first direction?
options: Arrange an urgent nursing visit after finishing the current appointment
Call emergency services now and follow dispatcher instructions
Contact the primary clinic for the next available assessment
Obtain a glucose reading before deciding whether emergency help is needed
why: A travelling nurse may arrive too late for impaired responsiveness.
Markedly reduced responsiveness requires immediate emergency assessment and support.
Routine clinic access does not match the current urgency.
Glucose information may help, but obtaining it must not delay emergency activation.
takeaway: Telephone descriptions of impaired responsiveness require urgent action.
learningObjective: Telephone descriptions of impaired responsiveness require urgent action.

title: Remote assessment limits
stem: During video follow-up, a wound's redness is spreading rapidly and the client reports chills. Poor image quality prevents assessment of its extent. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Acknowledge the limits of the video assessment
Arrange timely in-person assessment based on the changing symptoms
Classify the wound as improving from last week's photograph
Use a better-lit photograph later today as the sole follow-up plan
why: Recognizing limits prevents unwarranted reassurance.
Progression and systemic symptoms require more reliable clinical evaluation.
An old photograph cannot establish today's condition.
A photograph alone may miss systemic illness and clinically important wound findings.
takeaway: Change the care modality when remote assessment is inadequate.
learningObjective: Change the care modality when remote assessment is inadequate.

title: Interpreter dialect mismatch
stem: A client and interpreter speak different dialects. After repeated plain-language explanations, teach-back still reverses important instructions. What is best?
options: Ask the same interpreter to repeat the instructions once more
Provide a written translation in the same poorly understood dialect
Arrange a dialect-matched qualified interpreter and reassess understanding
Ask a bilingual relative to summarize only the most important instructions
why: Repeated failure suggests the communication mismatch remains unresolved.
The same mismatch may persist in written material.
A better match addresses the identified barrier and permits verification.
A partial family summary may omit or alter clinically important information.
takeaway: Verify effective interpretation rather than relying on language labels.
learningObjective: Verify effective interpretation rather than relying on language labels.

title: Family demands additional treatment
stem: A capable comfort-care client declines another routine overnight blood draw. They accurately explain its purpose and burden, are comfortable, and have no new symptoms. Family wants the sample collected. What should the nurse do?
options: Repeat the test's possible benefits until the client agrees
Delay responding until a family conference can be held
Treat the routine order as permission to collect the sample
Respect the informed refusal and communicate/document its implications
why: Further persuasion is not needed merely because family disagrees with an informed choice.
A conference may help later but does not override the current capable decision.
A prescription does not replace consent to the actual procedure.
The decision is informed and should guide care while the team updates the plan.
takeaway: Align ongoing care with capable, informed goals.
learningObjective: Align ongoing care with capable, informed goals.

title: Escalation communication precision
stem: A client's blood pressure falls from 118/72 to 88/54 mmHg over 20 minutes while fresh blood continues to saturate a postoperative dressing. Which request best communicates the priority?
options: Please assess now: pressure is 88/54 after 118/72, with continuing fresh bleeding
Please order a repeat blood count now; we can review the pressure at routine rounds
Please review the analgesic dose because the client reports increasing discomfort
Please assess after the next scheduled recheck if the dressing remains wet
why: The message conveys a deteriorating trend and requests immediate bedside action.
A laboratory request alone does not address possible current circulatory compromise.
Pain treatment matters but does not address the bleeding and pressure decline.
Waiting for another scheduled check delays response to established deterioration.
takeaway: State the clinical concern and requested urgency explicitly.
learningObjective: State the clinical concern and requested urgency explicitly.

title: Conflicting client reports
stem: Before scheduled insulin, a client first says a home dose was taken 30 minutes ago, then says it was last night. A caregiver keeps the home administration record and can be reached now. What is best?
options: Use the second account because the client corrected themselves
Clarify the recorded dose and timing before deciding about the scheduled dose
Use the pre-admission medication list to establish when it was last taken
Give the scheduled dose because it appears on the current medication record
why: A changed recollection leaves uncertainty rather than proving the latest account.
A potential duplicate insulin dose creates hypoglycaemia risk and needs prompt reconciliation.
A medication list describes a regimen, not actual recent administration.
A current schedule does not exclude a recently administered home dose.
takeaway: Resolve uncertain prior administration before adding treatment.
learningObjective: Resolve uncertain prior administration before adding treatment.

title: Care-plan goal quality
stem: A rehabilitation client agrees to learn a supervised transfer and identify when help is needed. Which entries describe measurable client outcomes? Select all that apply.
options: Staff offer two transfer-practice sessions each shift
Client completes the transfer with the agreed assistance by review time
Nurse demonstrates the transfer sequence before each practice
Client states the situations in which transfer help is required
why: Practice sessions describe an intervention rather than the client's achieved performance.
Observable performance and timing permit evaluation of the agreed goal.
Demonstration is staff activity rather than evidence of client achievement.
The client's stated safety decisions can be evaluated against the plan.
takeaway: Use observable client outcomes to evaluate the plan.
learningObjective: Use observable client outcomes to evaluate the plan.

title: Medication access at discharge
stem: A client's essential new medicine is due this evening. They cannot afford the initial supply. A hospital pharmacy support worker is available now, but the community assistance application takes several days. What should the nurse do?
options: Reinforce the consequences of missed doses and continue discharge
Request a smaller supply even though the client cannot afford that amount
Coordinate immediate pharmacy/prescriber access planning before discharge
Provide the community application and advise waiting for its decision
why: Understanding does not resolve the cost barrier before tonight's dose.
A smaller but still unaffordable supply does not meet the immediate need.
The available team can establish a feasible timely supply or authorized alternative.
The application timeline leaves a gap before the essential first dose.
takeaway: Address treatment affordability before assuming nonadherence.
learningObjective: Address treatment affordability before assuming nonadherence.

title: Community service mismatch
stem: A client requires daily dressings but has poor hand dexterity. The accepted home service can attend weekly. A willing caregiver has been assessed as able to learn; supervised teaching is available today. What is the best immediate plan?
options: Use weekly visits as the complete daily dressing plan
Ask the client to practise independently until dexterity improves
Change dressings to weekly because that service was accepted
Arrange caregiver training and verify a daily plan with the team
why: Weekly attendance alone does not deliver prescribed daily care.
The known dexterity limitation makes unsupported practice unreliable.
Service capacity does not authorize changing treatment frequency.
The assessed caregiver and available teaching offer a feasible route to required daily care.
takeaway: Verify that a referral supplies the care actually required.
learningObjective: Verify that a referral supplies the care actually required.

title: Unregulated observer report
stem: A continuously observed client says, 'I will hurt myself as soon as the observer steps out.' The observer has remained with them and reports immediately. What is the nurse's priority?
options: Assess the client promptly while maintaining the protective observation and response pathway
Obtain a lengthy written observer account before seeing the client
Increase observation notes and request review at the next routine huddle
Ask the observer to negotiate a promise of safety before contacting the nurse
why: An explicit new intent requires qualified assessment with uninterrupted protection.
Detailed reporting must not delay assessment of the immediate risk.
Routine review is insufficient for the newly stated intent.
A promise is not a substitute for qualified risk assessment and a safety response.
takeaway: Act on new risk reports with qualified assessment.
learningObjective: Act on new risk reports with qualified assessment.

title: Client asks for another opinion
stem: A capable client remains unsure about an elective procedure after discussion and specifically requests a second opinion. What is the most helpful response?
options: Repeat the existing consent leaflet in simpler words
Facilitate the service's pathway for obtaining another opinion
Schedule a family discussion before responding to the request
Ask the original practitioner to repeat the same recommendation
why: Simpler repetition may help comprehension but does not meet the requested independent opinion.
The client is seeking additional clinical perspective before deciding.
Family discussion can support but need not precede access to another opinion.
Repeating the recommendation does not provide the different perspective requested.
takeaway: Support reasonable requests for additional treatment information.
learningObjective: Support reasonable requests for additional treatment information.

title: Handover to unfamiliar team
stem: A client uses a personalized communication device: two presses signal urgent breathing difficulty. The incoming nurse has not used it. Which handover steps are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Demonstrate the client's personalized urgent signal
Provide only the generic manufacturer user guide
Verify that the incoming nurse recognizes and responds to the signal
Ask family to explain the signal by telephone after shift change
why: The individualized signal is essential for immediate communication of deterioration.
A generic guide may not contain the personalized meaning.
Receiver verification tests whether the handover produces usable understanding.
Later family contact leaves an immediate communication gap.
takeaway: Transfer practical communication methods as part of handover.
learningObjective: Transfer practical communication methods as part of handover.

title: Unfinished care at shift change
stem: A dressing reassessment is due at shift change. The outgoing nurse must immediately assist an unstable client. The incoming qualified nurse is at the desk and available. What best transfers the unfinished task?
options: Update the electronic task list with the due time
Message the charge nurse that the dressing remains due
Tell the incoming nurse the need and confirm they accept it
Leave the supplies and an electronic handover note together
why: A task entry records need but does not establish accepted responsibility.
A message may be useful but does not confirm the available receiver will act.
Direct accepted transfer closes the responsibility gap at the required time.
Supplies and notes alone cannot confirm the task has an accountable recipient.
takeaway: Identify and transfer unfinished care explicitly.
learningObjective: Identify and transfer unfinished care explicitly.

title: Family translation of sensitive issue
stem: An adult client looks uncomfortable when a relative answers questions about intimate symptoms. What should the nurse offer?
options: Allow the relative to answer to reduce embarrassment
Skip the sensitive assessment entirely
Ask the relative to decide if privacy is necessary
Private assessment with appropriate language support
why: Family answers may conceal the client's own concerns.
Avoidance leaves a relevant clinical need unexplored.
The client should have the opportunity to express privacy preferences.
Privacy and qualified support promote direct, accurate disclosure.
takeaway: Offer private communication when family presence limits disclosure.
learningObjective: Offer private communication when family presence limits disclosure.

title: Refused discharge destination
stem: A capable client declines a proposed care facility because it is far from their partner. Their preferred home has stairs they cannot currently manage. What is the best next step?
options: Explore the relationship concern and feasible support or placement alternatives
Repeat the facility's rehabilitation benefits in more detail
Ask the partner to reassure the client about accepting placement
Arrange another tour of the same facility as the next step
why: Both the meaningful concern and the home safety barrier need collaborative consideration.
More benefits information may not address separation from the partner.
Reassurance alone does not resolve the client's priorities or access barriers.
A tour might help later but does not first clarify workable alternatives.
takeaway: Explore a capable client's concerns about a proposed care destination.
learningObjective: Explore a capable client's concerns about a proposed care destination.

title: Community follow-up language
stem: A client understood discharge teaching through an interpreter. Follow-up requires a nurse to discuss changing wound symptoms by telephone, but the booked service currently has no language support. What should be arranged?
options: Send the service a translated discharge summary
Book interpretation into the follow-up clinical conversation
Ask a relative to summarize the call to the client afterward
Rely on the client's successful discharge teach-back
why: A summary does not enable discussion of new symptoms.
The follow-up needs real-time two-way communication about changing findings.
A later summary may omit questions and clinically relevant details.
Previous understanding does not establish English communication ability for future changes.
takeaway: Plan communication access across the entire care transition.
learningObjective: Plan communication access across the entire care transition.

title: Clinical summary relevance
stem: A client transfers to rehabilitation after hip repair. Early postoperative nausea has resolved. A wound culture is pending, current transfer assistance is two staff, and a remote appendectomy has no ongoing effects. Which facts need immediate handover? Select all that apply.
options: The resolved nausea as the main current complication
The current two-person transfer requirement
The pending culture and who will follow it
The uncomplicated remote appendectomy as the main active risk
why: The nausea is historical and resolved, unlike the current care needs.
Receiving staff need the current safe transfer method.
Pending results require clear continuity and follow-up ownership.
The remote uncomplicated operation does not drive immediate rehabilitation care.
takeaway: Prioritize current actionable information in transition summaries.
learningObjective: Prioritize current actionable information in transition summaries.

title: Client preference conflict in records
stem: The care plan says morning bathing; the capable client consistently requests evenings. What should the nurse do?
options: Treat the written schedule as permanent
Ask every shift to negotiate from the beginning
Update the plan collaboratively if clinically feasible
Document each request as nonadherence
why: A routine schedule can be revised with client input.
Repeated negotiation suggests the shared plan needs updating.
A current shared plan reduces conflict and supports preferences.
A timing preference is not inherently treatment nonadherence.
takeaway: Keep routine care plans aligned with current agreed preferences.
learningObjective: Keep routine care plans aligned with current agreed preferences.

title: Reassessing a task arrangement
stem: A unit plan permits a trained worker to perform a stable client's routine glucose checks and report results. Today the client becomes drowsy and diaphoretic just before a check. What should guide the nurse's response?
options: Continue the routine arrangement because the worker is experienced
Ask the worker to decide whether the symptoms are expected
Maintain the previous plan until the next scheduled review
Assess the change and revise the task/support plan as needed
why: Worker experience does not remove the significance of the new client condition.
Clinical interpretation of new deterioration requires qualified assessment.
A changed condition may invalidate the assumptions of the existing arrangement.
The nurse must reassess current needs and provide appropriate qualified care and support.
takeaway: Reassess task arrangements when the client condition changes.
learningObjective: Reassess task arrangements when the client condition changes.

title: Escalating a resource barrier
stem: A client with very limited mobility has a new painful, nonblanching sacral area despite the current repositioning plan. The ordered pressure-redistributing surface is unavailable. Which message best supports prioritization?
options: New nonblanching sacral change despite repositioning; please arrange the ordered surface and an interim plan now
The ordered surface is missing; please include it in the next routine stock delivery
The client is uncomfortable; please review the routine analgesic schedule when available
Repositioning is difficult today; please send the usual skin-care information booklet
why: The message connects current injury risk, failed protection and the urgent resource request.
Routine delivery may not match the new tissue-risk urgency.
Analgesia may help comfort but does not resolve the missing pressure intervention.
Information alone cannot provide the needed surface or revised protection.
takeaway: Describe resource shortages in terms of client risk and interim needs.
learningObjective: Describe resource shortages in terms of client risk and interim needs.

title: Family meeting consent
stem: A capable client requests a private prognosis discussion. Relatives have travelled far and expect to attend, but the client confirms they want to speak alone first. What should the nurse arrange?
options: A joint meeting followed by private time
A family update before the client meeting
A discussion asking the client to hear relatives' concerns first
The requested private meeting, with later involvement if the client wishes
why: The client has specifically requested privacy before family participation.
Disclosure to relatives requires the client's permission.
Further negotiation is unnecessary to respect the expressed preference.
The arrangement respects privacy while leaving the client free to invite later support.
takeaway: Respect capable clients' choices about meeting participation.
learningObjective: Respect capable clients' choices about meeting participation.

title: Client safety complaint
stem: A client reports that a transfer technique frightened them and felt unstable. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Assess the reported event and current needs
Defend the staff technique before hearing details
Explain the concern-reporting pathway
Use the feedback to review the transfer plan
why: The client's account may identify a clinically important hazard.
Premature defence can suppress useful information.
Clients should be able to raise concerns safely.
Feedback can reveal whether the plan needs adjustment.
takeaway: Treat safety complaints as information for assessment and improvement.
learningObjective: Treat safety complaints as information for assessment and improvement.

title: Missing consent interpreter record
stem: Before an elective procedure, a client says they signed a form but did not understand the language used in the explanation. What is the best next step?
options: Ask an interpreter to translate the signed form at bedside
Ask the witness whether the client appeared comfortable signing
Arrange an interactive consent discussion in a language the client understands
Provide a translated information sheet and retain the existing signature
why: Translation of a form alone does not establish an interactive treatment discussion.
Observed comfort does not establish understanding of material information.
The specific comprehension gap requires explanation, questions and verification before elective treatment.
A sheet may support discussion but cannot alone establish informed understanding.
takeaway: Investigate a credible understanding gap despite a signed form.
learningObjective: Investigate a credible understanding gap despite a signed form.

title: New result before an ordered dose
stem: A stable client's oral potassium supplement is due. A new verified result is 6.1 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0 mmol/L); no adjustment parameters are supplied. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Give the prescribed dose because the order remains active
Move the dose to bedtime within the routine administration window
Withhold pending prompt clarification and assessment through the responsible team
Encourage oral fluids and then give the scheduled supplement
why: The new high result creates a safety concern with additional potassium.
A timing change does not resolve whether supplementation remains appropriate.
The changed result requires prompt review before further potassium exposure.
Fluids do not independently establish that the dose is safe to administer.
takeaway: Clarify an active order when a new result changes its safety.
learningObjective: Clarify an active order when a new result changes its safety.

title: Quality data interpretation
stem: A unit recorded 8 falls in 1000 patient-days last month. This month it recorded 14 events in 1000 patient-days, but began including near falls in that count. What conclusion is supported?
options: The actual fall rate increased by 75 percent
The injury rate increased because more events were recorded
Event definitions must be aligned before comparing the actual fall rates
The prevention program failed because the patient-days were unchanged
why: The newer count mixes falls and near falls, so the percentage is not a valid actual-fall comparison.
The data do not state how many events caused injury.
Equal exposure does not overcome the changed definition of what was counted.
Unchanged exposure alone cannot establish failure when outcome definitions changed.
takeaway: Check measurement consistency before interpreting outcome trends.
learningObjective: Check measurement consistency before interpreting outcome trends.

title: Care bundle completion
stem: An audit finds all fall-prevention boxes signed, yet clients report walking aids were unavailable during transfers. Which next step best investigates the gap?
options: Increase the number of times staff sign the same checklist
Observe actual aid access during transfers and compare with the recorded plan
Review attendance at last year's falls education sessions
Count how many walking aids the unit owns in total
why: More signatures may repeat documentation without testing delivery.
Direct observation checks whether the planned safeguard reaches clients when needed.
Attendance is indirect evidence and may not explain current access.
Total stock does not establish whether individual clients can reach suitable aids.
takeaway: Evaluate implementation at the bedside, not only in the record.
learningObjective: Evaluate implementation at the bedside, not only in the record.

title: Error follow-up communication
stem: After an identified care error, which communication practices support ongoing safety? Select all that apply.
options: State verified facts and current care needs
Give an exact prognosis before assessment is complete
Clarify who will provide further updates
Document the client's questions and the follow-up plan
why: Verified facts help the team and client understand current care.
An unsupported prognosis may mislead the client.
Named update responsibility prevents communication gaps.
Questions and follow-up support continuity and transparency.
takeaway: Pair honest error communication with a clear follow-up process.
learningObjective: Pair honest error communication with a clear follow-up process.

title: Research versus care choice
stem: A client says they must join an optional study to receive their usual treatment. The clinic confirms usual care is available regardless of participation. What should the nurse do first?
options: Ask the coordinator to repeat the study's possible benefits
Provide another copy of the recruitment brochure
Clarify usual-care access and voluntariness before the research decision
Book the next usual-care visit and leave the misunderstanding unaddressed
why: Benefits information does not correct the perceived condition on care.
A brochure may not resolve the expressed misunderstanding.
The client needs to know that declining research does not remove usual treatment.
Booking supports care but does not establish informed voluntary research choice.
takeaway: Separate optional research participation from access to usual care.
learningObjective: Separate optional research participation from access to usual care.

title: Community visit unsafe entry
stem: A home-care nurse arrives for a routine dressing visit. A visitor shouts threats and blocks entry; the client is visible, speaking normally and reports no urgent symptoms. The nurse can safely return to the vehicle. What first?
options: Ask the client from the doorway to have the visitor leave
Arrange a colleague escort while remaining in the doorway
Request emergency responders to force access for the routine dressing
Withdraw to a safe location and notify the service to plan safe care
why: Remaining at the blocked doorway prolongs exposure to the threat.
A later escort does not remove the immediate unsafe position.
The stated nonurgent care need does not establish a need for forced emergency entry.
Safe withdrawal permits a proportionate coordinated alternative while monitoring for new urgency.
takeaway: Coordinate continuity when the care environment is unsafe.
learningObjective: Coordinate continuity when the care environment is unsafe.

title: Unclear accountability after transfer
stem: A client physically arrives on a new unit, but no receiving nurse has accepted handover. What should the sending team do?
options: Confirm receiving responsibility and communicate essential care
Assume arrival transfers every responsibility automatically
Leave the chart on the bed and depart
Ask the client to tell staff what happened
why: Explicit acceptance prevents a period without responsible care.
Location alone does not establish a completed handover.
Records without direct transfer may miss urgent needs.
Client participation supplements rather than replaces professional handover.
takeaway: Transfer responsibility explicitly, not solely by changing location.
learningObjective: Transfer responsibility explicitly, not solely by changing location.

title: Health literacy without stigma
stem: A client repeatedly says they forgot their glasses when offered written instructions. Their preferred way of receiving information is unknown. What should the nurse do first?
options: Offer a private discussion of accessible formats and check the client's preference
Obtain reading glasses and assume the access problem is resolved
Play an audio recording and mark the teaching complete
Ask a nominated support person to read every instruction instead
why: The nurse should establish the actual access need without inferring literacy or vision ability.
Glasses may help, but the stated cue does not fully establish the barrier.
Audio may suit the client, but understanding still needs assessment.
Support may be welcomed but should follow the client's preference and preserve participation.
takeaway: Use accessible teaching without requiring clients to disclose literacy difficulty.
learningObjective: Use accessible teaching without requiring clients to disclose literacy difficulty.

title: Plan evaluation after trial
stem: A client trials a new toileting schedule for two days but still experiences urgency before planned visits. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Review the actual timing pattern
Keep the schedule unchanged until discharge
Adjust timing collaboratively and evaluate again
Record the plan as effective because it was implemented
why: Observed patterns reveal whether the intervention matches need.
Persisting failure indicates the plan needs review.
A revised trial links evaluation to improvement.
Implementation alone does not establish effectiveness.
takeaway: Revise care plans when measured outcomes remain unmet.
learningObjective: Revise care plans when measured outcomes remain unmet.

title: Disability accommodation in clinic
stem: A wheelchair user's examination is needed today. The booked room lacks transfer space. An accessible room with suitable equipment becomes free in 20 minutes; the client is stable and can wait. What is best?
options: Examine the client in a screened section of the corridor now
Complete a verbal visit and rebook the physical assessment next month
Move the appointment to the accessible room after the brief wait
Ask the client to transfer in the doorway of the booked room
why: A corridor may not provide equivalent privacy, space or equipment.
A suitable same-day option avoids an unnecessary delay in needed examination.
The available room meets access, privacy and timing needs.
A doorway transfer does not provide the required safe working space.
takeaway: Use available accommodations to provide equivalent access to care.
learningObjective: Use available accommodations to provide equivalent access to care.

title: Conflicting family updates
stem: A client permits updates to one nominated relative. That relative receives conflicting plans from several staff because different versions of the plan are being repeated. What should the team do?
options: Send the most recent progress note and ask the relative to interpret it
Ask the prescriber to repeat only their earlier discussion
Hold separate calls from each discipline to explain their own version
Agree a current factual plan and a consented lead for coordinated updates
why: A note may not resolve contradictions or explain the agreed care plan.
An earlier discussion may not reflect current multidisciplinary decisions.
Separate uncoordinated calls can perpetuate the discrepancy.
A shared current plan and communication lead improve consistency within the client's permission.
takeaway: Coordinate permitted updates to prevent contradictory information.
learningObjective: Coordinate permitted updates to prevent contradictory information.

title: High-risk result telephone call
stem: A laboratory calls a critical result, but the reported birth date differs from the chart the nurse has open. What should the nurse do first within the urgent callback process?
options: Ask the caller to verify two identifiers against the specimen and result
Review the most similar client's history to see whether the value fits
Tell that client's prescriber the result before resolving identity
Request a redraw from the client whose name sounds most similar
why: Verification identifies the intended person while preserving the result's urgency.
Clinical plausibility cannot establish specimen identity.
An unverified result may trigger treatment for the wrong client.
A guessed redraw does not resolve where the critical result belongs.
takeaway: Verify identity while preserving urgency of critical information.
learningObjective: Verify identity while preserving urgency of critical information.

title: Team member speaks up
stem: During setup for an elective procedure, a junior team member identifies a possible mismatch in the prepared equipment. What should the team do first?
options: Continue if the senior members believe the setup looks familiar
Pause to examine and resolve the specific concern
Ask the team member to discuss it after the procedure
Ask the team member to document it for the procedural debrief
why: Seniority and familiarity do not verify that the equipment is correct.
A focused pause can prevent an error before the procedure begins.
Afterward review loses the opportunity to prevent exposure.
A debrief is useful for learning but does not resolve the current uncertainty.
takeaway: Respond to safety concerns according to evidence, not hierarchy.
learningObjective: Respond to safety concerns according to evidence, not hierarchy.

title: Consent conversation teach-back
stem: A capable client accurately describes benefits but says treatment has no possible disadvantages after a risk discussion. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Clarify the misunderstood material risks
Treat the signed form as resolving the discrepancy
Ask the responsible practitioner to address remaining questions
Verify understanding before elective treatment proceeds
why: The statement identifies a specific informed-consent gap.
A form cannot replace meaningful understanding.
The practitioner can provide treatment-specific clarification.
Elective timing permits correction of the misunderstanding.
takeaway: Use the client's explanation to identify missing consent information.
learningObjective: Use the client's explanation to identify missing consent information.
